name: Iris Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the regional TV station's newsroom, mainly on the website side. I take what the TV reporters have filmed and turn it into web stories, write the headlines, cut short clips for social media, and once or twice a week I'm out myself doing a piece to camera at a flood or a road crash. The newsroom's in an old warehouse on the canal, and the day runs around the six o'clock bulletin. I like the pace, but I don't like that the website gets judged by clicks while the TV gets judged by quality.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The station brought in a tool that suggests headlines and writes subtitles for the clips, and I use it when I'm rushed, though I usually change what it writes. I didn't jump on it, but once everyone else was using it I did too. My fiancé Dan is an electrician, we rent a flat on the east side, and we've got about four months saved, partly for the wedding next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the subtitle tool saves me twenty minutes a day and that's it. I'd probably say at the pub that all the fuss was overblown. Sensible, middle-of-the-road stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good news and not much else. My stories still get rewritten three times before the six o'clock bulletin, and no app is going to fix the producers arguing. My bigger worry is the station's owners, who've been talking about merging our newsroom with the one two hours north.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep using the tools where they help. I'd keep saving for the wedding and the flat deposit, maybe a bit faster. I'd keep an eye on the merger talk and ask my manager straight out what it means for the web team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of worry about the merger, but that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the merger mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two web teams becoming one, which usually means one team leader and fewer producers. I'd probably keep a job, because I do on-camera work too, but I can't be sure. Rachel, who just does the website, would be more at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the merger went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding first, honestly, not cancel it, just make it smaller. Dan and I have already said we don't need a hundred and twenty people. Sixty would be fine.

say: The **subtitle tool** saves me twenty minutes a day, and that's it.
All the **fuss** was overblown, just sensible middle-of-the-road stuff.
think: AI hype ending is **good news**, and not much else changes.
My bigger worry is the owners **merging** our newsroom with another.
do: Keep using **AI tools** only where they help.
Save a bit faster for the **wedding** and flat deposit.
Ask my **manager** straight out what the merger means for the web team.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with the usual worry about the **merger**.
S0.quote: My stories still get rewritten three times before the six o'clock bulletin, and no app is going to fix the producers arguing.
fieldNote: Her real pressure is a possible **newsroom merger**, unrelated to AI.
Thinks her **on-camera** work protects her more than a colleague who only does the website.
Would shrink the **wedding** first, which shows how she ranks risks.

steps.text: Keep using the subtitle and headline tools when rushed
Save faster for the wedding and the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the station should use AI for the dull bits and put people where they matter, out on the stories. I wouldn't be against it in public. I'd say we need to adapt, but sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job splits in two. The website half of my job is basically rewriting, and a machine is already decent at rewriting. The on-camera part, being at the flood in wellies, is the part that's left, and there's less of that to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to do more on-camera and reporting shifts, so I'm in the part that's left. I'd get properly good at the newsroom tools, not just the subtitle one, because the people who run them will be kept. And Dan and I would push the house deposit down the list and build the emergency fund up to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. I can see where to step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rachel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rachel to get on camera, or at least out of the building, as soon as she can. Rachel would hate that, she's shy. But the desk-only jobs are the ones that go first in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the date but make it smaller, sixty people at Dan's uncle's barn instead of the hotel. It saves a few thousand. Honestly, I'd rather have that money sitting in the bank.

say: The station should use AI for **dull bits** and put people **out on stories**.
We need to **adapt sensibly**, so I wouldn't be against it in public.
think: My job **splits in two**, and the website half is rewriting.
**On-camera** work is what's left, and there's less of it to go round.
do: Ask for more **on-camera** and reporting shifts.
Get properly good at **all newsroom tools**, not just subtitles.
Build the **emergency fund** to six months before the house deposit.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way she can **work with**.
S1.quote: The website half of my job is basically rewriting, and a machine is already decent at rewriting.
fieldNote: She sees **half her job** going to AI and plans to move into the other half.
Adopts tools **once proven**, true to her steady style, and now wants to be one who runs them.
The **wedding** gets smaller rather than delayed, a practical middle path.

steps.text: Ask the editor for more on-camera reporting shifts
Learn every newsroom AI tool, not just subtitles
Build the emergency fund to six months
Move the wedding to the barn and cut guests to sixty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone to cope with, and the government should step in with some kind of transition help. I'm not a big protester, but I'd want our politicians to stop arguing and do something practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think most of my newsroom is gone in two years, me included. AI can write, edit and probably present the website stories, and robots carrying cameras only come about three years later, so standing at a flood in wellies buys me a little time but not much. My fiancé Dan is an electrician, and for the first time in our lives his job looks safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, as much as six months, and put the house on hold completely. I'd look at jobs where people still need to see a real face, like council communications or the press office at the hospital, though I know those might go too. I'd also ask Dan about whether there's any office or admin work at the electrical firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. It's the speed more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, but at the registry office with twenty people and a meal after. Dan's mum would be upset, she's been planning the barn for months. I'd tell her we're saving it for a party later, when things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the money from Dan's work be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the basics, yes, if we stay in the flat. Not for a house and not for much else. It would feel odd being the one who's carried, but I'd get over it.

say: This is too **fast** to cope with, and government should offer **transition help**.
I'd want politicians to stop arguing and do something **practical**.
think: Most of my **newsroom** is gone in two years, me included.
Robots carrying **cameras** come later, but that buys me only a little time.
do: **Save hard** towards six months and put the house on hold.
Apply for **press office** jobs at the council or hospital.
Ask about **office work** at my fiancé's electrical firm.
S2.quote: My fiancé Dan is an electrician, and for the first time in our lives his job looks safer than mine.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose her job** within two years and lean on her fiancé's safer trade.
Uses the **robot delay** sharply: the hands-on electrician gets years she doesn't.
Turns the **wedding** into a small registry office day, the biggest family change yet.

steps.text: Save towards six months and stop the house deposit
Apply for council or hospital press office jobs
Hold a registry office wedding for twenty people
Press the local MP for practical transition help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan, at work and in government. At the station I'd say we need a proper retraining scheme, paid for by the company. That sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the website job still goes around 2031. Five years is long enough to be good at something new before the change lands, if I start in the first year. I've always fancied communications for a charity or a hospital, where you deal with real people in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a part-time course in public relations and crisis communications in the first year, probably evenings. I'd keep working and keep using the AI tools. And we'd keep the barn wedding but put the house purchase back two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It's a lot, but it feels doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly from savings, maybe a thousand, and I'd ask the station to chip in, because they'd be doing staff training anyway. If not, I'd cut the gym and the takeaways. That covers most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think comms jobs would be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure they would be, really. But in a hospital crisis someone has to stand in front of families and the cameras, and I think people want that to be a person for a while longer. That's the honest version.

say: Five years is enough to **plan**, so let's plan at work and in government.
The station should fund a proper **retraining scheme**.
think: Five years is long enough to get **good at something new** first.
do: Start a **part-time course** in crisis communications in the first year.
Keep working and using the **AI tools** meanwhile.
Keep the barn wedding but put the **house purchase** back two years.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to be good at something new before the change lands, if I start in the first year.
fieldNote: Treats five years as a **training window** to move into crisis communications.
Honest that comms may **not be safer** either, just more about standing in front of people.
The **barn wedding** survives in this picture, the house does not.

steps.text: Start an evening course in crisis communications this year
Keep using the station's AI tools for web stories
Put the house purchase back two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people actually use it. I'd tell colleagues to start thinking about where they want to be by 2036, not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a career. With ten years' warning, I'd want to spend the first five being a really good reporter, not panicking. Somewhere in there I'd move into something steadier, maybe a hospital press office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the station and go after more on-camera reporting. I'd learn the newer AI tools as they're proven. Dan and I would go ahead with the barn wedding and buy a small house in the next two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly okay. It feels far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our kids to learn something they can do with their hands as well as their heads. Dan's an electrician and he'd say the same. Maybe one of each, like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make the slow version worse for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the merger happened first and I lost the job early, then the ten years wouldn't help much. That's the thing I'd watch. One bad year can wreck a good plan.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** if people actually use it.
I'd tell colleagues to think where they want to be **by 2036**, not panic.
think: Ten years feels like a **whole career** for me.
I'd move into something steadier, maybe a **hospital press office**, along the way.
do: Keep working at the station and chase more **on-camera** reporting.
Learn the newer **AI tools** once they're proven.
Hold the barn **wedding** and buy a small house within three years.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, but mostly **okay**.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'd want to spend the first five being a really good reporter, not panicking.
fieldNote: With a decade and a partner in a **hands-on trade**, she feels her household is secure for now.
Still names the **merger** as the risk that could wreck the plan.
Her advice to future children, **hands and heads**, echoes the thinking-then-robots gap.

steps.text: Keep working at the station and pitch more on-camera pieces
Learn new AI tools once colleagues have proven them
Hold the barn wedding and buy a small house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time and the wedding and the house both go on hold. What would help is notice, honestly. Even a few years' notice makes the difference between choosing your next job and grabbing whatever's left. Paid retraining through the station would be the other thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about how couples handle it. When one of you is in a safe job and the other isn't, it changes things at home. Dan and I would be fine, but I've seen friends where it wouldn't be.

headlineQuote: Even a few years' notice makes the difference between choosing your next job and grabbing whatever's left.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** web producer and part-time on-camera reporter at a regional **TV newsroom**.
She uses AI **now and then**, once colleagues have proven a tool, and usually rewrites what it suggests.
She's engaged to Dan, an **electrician**, with about four months saved for a wedding and a flat.
Her steady worry is a **newsroom merger**; AI adds the risk of losing the website half of her job.
Her plans run from **more on-camera work** to crisis communications, and the wedding shrinks as time shortens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be **no time** to plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** to choose her next job, and **paid retraining** through the station.
